flashcards.title: Planck's Quantum Theory
formulas: Energy of one photon = hν = hc/λ
explanation: Planck's quantum theory explains the quantization of energy. It states that energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete amounts called quanta.

flashcards.title: Photoelectric Effect
explanation: The photoelectric effect describes the ejection of electrons from a metal surface when exposed to light of a certain minimum frequency.

flashcards.title: Bohr’s Model for Hydrogen-like Atoms
explanation: Bohr’s model introduced quantization of angular momentum and explained the discrete energy levels of hydrogen-like atoms.
The energy and radius of an electron's orbit depend on the principal quantum number (n) and the atomic number (Z).

flashcards.title: De-Broglie Wavelength
explanation: De-Broglie proposed that particles exhibit wave-like properties, with a wavelength inversely proportional to their momentum.

flashcards.title: Wavelength of Emitted Photon
explanation: The wavelength of light emitted during an electronic transition in hydrogen-like atoms is determined by the Rydberg formula.
R is the Rydberg constant, Z is the atomic number, and n₁ and n₂ are principal quantum numbers.

flashcards.title: No. of Photons Emitted by a Sample of H Atom
explanation: The number of photons emitted during transitions can be calculated using the given formula, where Δn is the change in the quantum number.

flashcards.title: Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle
explanation: The principle states that it is impossible to simultaneously determine the exact position and momentum of a particle.
It emphasizes the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics.

flashcards.title: Quantum Numbers
explanation: Quantum numbers define the state of an electron in an atom, including its energy, angular momentum, and orientation.
Principal quantum number (n): Energy level or shell.
Azimuthal quantum number (l): Shape of the orbital.
Magnetic quantum number (m): Orientation of the orbital.
Spin quantum number (s): Spin of the electron.

flashcards.title: Relative Atomic Mass (R.A.M)
formulas: R.A.M = Mass of one atom of an element / (1/12 × Mass of one carbon atom)
explanation: Relative atomic mass compares the mass of an atom to 1/12th the mass of a carbon atom.
It is a dimensionless quantity.

flashcards.title: Density
formulas: Specific Gravity = Density of the substance / Density of water at 4°C
explanation: Density is defined as mass per unit volume.
Specific gravity compares the density of a substance to the density of water.

flashcards.title: Concentration Terms
formulas: Molarity (M) = w × 1000 / (Mol. wt of solute × V in mL)
Molality (m) = Number of moles of solute / Mass of solvent in grams
explanation: Molarity is the number of moles of solute per liter of solution.
Molality is the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.
Mole fraction represents the ratio of moles of a component to the total moles in the mixture.

flashcards.title: Conversions and Derived Formulas
formulas: Mole Fraction of Solute to Molarity (M) = x₂ρ × 1000 / (x₁M₁ + x₂M₂)
Molarity to Mole Fraction (x₂) = M × M₁ / (1000ρ - MM₂)
Mole Fraction to Molality (m) = x₂ × 1000 / x₁M₁
explanation: These formulas allow the conversion between different concentration terms.

flashcards.title: Mean Atomic Mass
explanation: The mean atomic mass is the weighted average of the atomic masses of all isotopes of an element.

flashcards.title: Mean Molar Mass or Molecular Mass
explanation: The mean molecular mass is the weighted average of the molar masses of components in a mixture.

flashcards.title: Oxidation Number
formulas: Oxidation Number = Number of electrons in the valence shell - Number of electrons left after bonding
explanation: The oxidation number indicates the charge of an atom in a compound, considering the distribution of electrons.

flashcards.title: Equivalent Weight
formulas: E = Molar Mass / Basicity or Acidity
E = M / (Number of moles of e⁻ gained/lost)
explanation: Equivalent weight is the amount of a substance that combines with or displaces a fixed amount of another substance.

flashcards.title: Normality
formulas: Normality (N) = Number of equivalents of solute / Volume of solution in liters
explanation: Normality measures the concentration of equivalents of solute in a solution.

flashcards.title: Volume Strength of H₂O₂
explanation: Volume strength indicates the amount of oxygen released by hydrogen peroxide at standard temperature and pressure.

flashcards.title: Hardness of Water
formulas: Hardness in ppm = (Mass of CaCO₃ × 10⁶) / Total Mass of Water
explanation: Hardness of water is the concentration of calcium and magnesium salts, expressed in parts per million (ppm).

flashcards.title: Available Chlorine in Bleaching Powder
explanation: Available chlorine is the amount of chlorine released by bleaching powder during titration with a standard solution.

flashcards.title: Thermodynamic Processes
formulas: Isothermal Process: T = constant, dT = 0, ΔT = 0
Isochoric Process: V = constant, dV = 0, ΔV = 0
Isobaric Process: P = constant, dP = 0, ΔP = 0
Adiabatic Process: q = 0 (no heat exchange with the surroundings)
explanation: Thermodynamic processes describe how a system interacts with its surroundings during changes in pressure, volume, and temperature.

flashcards.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
formulas: Law of Equipartition of Energy: U = (f/2) nRT
explanation: The first law states that energy is conserved and can neither be created nor destroyed.
It is applied to calculate changes in internal energy, work, and heat exchange.

flashcards.title: Heat Capacity
formulas: Total Heat Capacity: Cₜ = (ΔQ / ΔT) = dq / dT (J/°C)
Molar Heat Capacity: Cₚ = dq / ndT (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Specific Heat Capacity: s = dq / mΔT = dq / mdT (J gm⁻¹ K⁻¹)
explanation: Heat capacity quantifies the heat required to raise the temperature of a substance by a certain amount.

flashcards.title: Work Done (w)
formulas: Isothermal Reversible Process: W = -nRT ln (V₂ / V₁)
Reversible Isobaric Process: W = P (V₂ - V₁)
explanation: Work done depends on the type of thermodynamic process and involves changes in volume or pressure.

flashcards.title: Second Law of Thermodynamics
formulas: ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surrounding > 0 (for a spontaneous process)
explanation: The second law states that the entropy of an isolated system always increases for a spontaneous process.

flashcards.title: Entropy for Ideal Gas
formulas: ΔS_system = nCₚ ln (T₂ / T₁) + nR ln (V₂ / V₁)
explanation: Entropy changes during processes involving gases depend on temperature and volume changes.

flashcards.title: Third Law of Thermodynamics
formulas: At absolute zero temperature, the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero.
explanation: This law states that entropy approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero for perfect crystalline substances.

flashcards.title: Gibb’s Free Energy (G)
explanation: Gibb's free energy determines the spontaneity of a process.
If ΔG < 0, the process is spontaneous.
If ΔG > 0, the process is non-spontaneous.

flashcards.title: Thermochemistry
formulas: ΔH° = H°ₘ₂ - H°ₘ₁ (heat added at constant pressure)
explanation: Thermochemistry deals with the heat changes accompanying chemical reactions.

flashcards.title: Kirchhoff's Equation
formulas: ΔH° = ΔH°₁ + ΔCₚ (T₂ - T₁) (at constant pressure)
ΔE° = ΔE°₁ + ∫ C_V dT (at constant volume)
explanation: Kirchhoff's equation relates changes in enthalpy to temperature changes.

flashcards.title: Resonance Energy
explanation: Resonance energy is the difference between experimental and calculated enthalpies of a molecule.

flashcards.title: Temperature Scale
explanation: Temperature conversion formulas for Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit.

flashcards.title: Boyle's Law and Measurement of Pressure
explanation: Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume.

flashcards.title: Charles' Law
explanation: Charles' law states that the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature at constant pressure.

flashcards.title: Gay-Lussac's Law
explanation: Gay-Lussac's law states that the pressure of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature at constant volume.

flashcards.title: Ideal Gas Equation
explanation: The ideal gas equation relates pressure, volume, temperature, and the amount of gas (in moles).

flashcards.title: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressure
formulas: Partial Pressure = Mole Fraction × Total Pressure
explanation: Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of each component.

flashcards.title: Amagat's Law of Partial Volume
explanation: Amagat's law states that the total volume of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial volumes of each component.

flashcards.title: Graham's Law
explanation: Graham's law states that the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass.

flashcards.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
formulas: Average K.E. for one mole = (3/2) K N_A T = (3/2) RT
explanation: The kinetic theory of gases relates the motion of gas molecules to macroscopic properties such as pressure and temperature.

flashcards.title: Van der Waal's Equation
formulas: Critical Constants: V_c = 3b, P_c = a/27b², T_c = 8a/27Rb
explanation: Van der Waal's equation accounts for intermolecular forces and the finite size of gas molecules, correcting the ideal gas law.

flashcards.title: At Equilibrium
formulas: Rate of forward reaction = Rate of backward reaction
Concentration (mol/litre) of reactant and product becomes constant
explanation: At equilibrium, the rates of the forward and backward reactions are equal, and there is no net change in concentrations.

flashcards.title: Equilibrium Constant (K)
formulas: K = Rate constant of forward reaction / Rate constant of backward reaction
explanation: The equilibrium constant quantifies the ratio of the concentrations of products to reactants at equilibrium.

flashcards.title: Equilibrium Constant in Terms of Concentration (K_c)
explanation: K_c is expressed in terms of the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium.

flashcards.title: Equilibrium Constant in Terms of Partial Pressure (K_p)
explanation: K_p is expressed in terms of the partial pressures of reactants and products at equilibrium.

flashcards.title: Equilibrium Constant in Terms of Mole Fraction (K_x)
explanation: K_x uses mole fractions to represent the equilibrium constant.

flashcards.title: Relation Between K_p, K_c, and K_x
explanation: These relationships connect the equilibrium constants expressed in different terms and account for changes in temperature.

flashcards.title: Reaction Quotient (Q)
explanation: The reaction quotient predicts the direction of the reaction's shift to reach equilibrium.

flashcards.title: Degree of Dissociation (α)
formulas: α = Number of moles dissociated / Initial number of moles taken
explanation: Degree of dissociation represents the fraction of moles dissociated into products.

flashcards.title: Effect of Temperature on Equilibrium
formulas: If ln K vs 1/T is plotted, slope = -ΔH°/R and intercept = ΔS°/R
explanation: For endothermic reactions (ΔH > 0), K increases with temperature.
For exothermic reactions (ΔH < 0), K decreases with temperature.

flashcards.title: Vapour Pressure of Liquid
formulas: Relative Humidity = Partial Pressure of H₂O Vapours / Vapour Pressure of H₂O at that Temp
explanation: Relative humidity compares the actual vapor pressure to the saturation vapor pressure at a given temperature.

flashcards.title: Thermodynamics of Equilibrium
explanation: Thermodynamics of equilibrium relates Gibbs free energy to equilibrium constants and temperature.

flashcards.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
explanation: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a disturbance (e.g., change in concentration, pressure, or temperature), it shifts to minimize the effect of the disturbance.

flashcards.title: Ostwald Dilution Law
explanation: Ostwald's dilution law relates the dissociation constant of a weak acid or base to its degree of dissociation and concentration.

flashcards.title: Acidity and pH Scale
explanation: The pH scale measures the acidity or basicity of a solution, with pH < 7 being acidic, pH > 7 being basic, and pH = 7 being neutral.

flashcards.title: Properties of Water
explanation: Water dissociates slightly to produce H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, and the ionic product (K_w) is constant at a given temperature.

flashcards.title: pH of Different Solutions
formulas: pH of a strong acid solution: [H⁺] = N
pH of a strong base solution: [OH⁻] = N
pH of a weak acid solution: K_a = Cα²
pH of a weak base solution: K_b = Cα²
pH of a mixture of two strong acids: [H⁺] = (N₁V₁ + N₂V₂) / (V₁ + V₂)
explanation: The pH of a solution depends on the strength and concentration of acids or bases present in the solution.

flashcards.title: Relative Strength of Two Acids
formulas: [H⁺] furnished by acid 1 / [H⁺] furnished by acid 2 = (K_a₁C₁) / (K_a₂C₂)
explanation: The strength of an acid is proportional to its dissociation constant (K_a) and its concentration.

flashcards.title: Salt Hydrolysis
formulas: For weak acid + strong base: pH = 7 + 1/2 pK_a + 1/2 log C
For strong acid + weak base: pH = 7 - 1/2 pK_b - 1/2 log C
For weak acid + weak base: pH = 7 + 1/2 (pK_a - pK_b)
explanation: Salt hydrolysis involves the reaction of salt with water to produce acidic or basic solutions depending on the type of salt.

flashcards.title: Buffer Solutions
formulas: For acidic buffer: pH = pK_a + log ([Salt] / [Acid])
For basic buffer: pOH = pK_b + log ([Salt] / [Base])
explanation: Buffer solutions resist changes in pH upon addition of small amounts of acid or base.

flashcards.title: Solubility Product (K_sp)
formulas: Condition for precipitation: Ionic product (K_ip) > K_sp
explanation: The solubility product represents the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a sparingly soluble salt.

flashcards.title: Electrode Potential
formulas: E_cell = R.P of cathode - R.P of anode
E_cell = O.P of anode - O.P of cathode
E_cell = SRP of cathode - SRP of anode
explanation: Electrode potential measures the tendency of an electrode to lose or gain electrons.
The standard reduction potential (SRP) is used to determine the direction of electron flow.

flashcards.title: Gibbs Free Energy Change
explanation: The Gibbs free energy change relates the work done by an electrochemical cell to the cell potential and the number of electrons involved.

flashcards.title: Nernst Equation
explanation: The Nernst equation calculates the cell potential at non-standard conditions.
It accounts for the effect of reactant and product concentrations on the cell potential.

flashcards.title: Concentration Cell
explanation: Concentration cells generate emf based on concentration differences of the same material in two half-cells.

flashcards.title: Different Types of Electrodes
formulas: Metal-Metal Ion Electrode: E = E° + (0.0591/n) log [M⁺]
Gas Ion Electrode: E = E° - (0.0591/n) log [H⁺]
Metal-Metal Insoluble Salt Electrode: E = E° - 0.0591 log [Cl⁻]
explanation: Different types of electrodes are used based on the reactions occurring at the electrode surface.

flashcards.title: Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis
formulas: Second Law: w/E = constant, w₁/E₁ = w₂/E₂
Current Efficiency = (Actual Mass Deposited / Theoretical Mass) × 100
explanation: Faraday's laws describe the relationship between the amount of substance deposited or liberated at an electrode and the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

flashcards.title: Conductance
formulas: Specific Conductance: K = 1/ρ (reciprocal of specific resistance)
explanation: Conductance measures the ability of a solution to conduct electricity.
It depends on the type and concentration of ions present in the solution.

flashcards.title: Kohlrausch's Law
explanation: Kohlrausch's law relates the molar conductivity of an electrolyte to its concentration.
It is used to calculate the degree of dissociation and solubility product of weak electrolytes.

flashcards.title: Transport Number
explanation: The transport number represents the fraction of the total current carried by a specific ion in an electrolyte.

flashcards.title: Raoult's Law for Binary (Ideal) Mixture of Volatile Liquids
formulas: P_T = P_A + P_B = X_A P_A° + X_B P_B°
explanation: Raoult's law states that the partial vapor pressure of each component in an ideal solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction.

flashcards.title: Elevation in Boiling Point
explanation: The boiling point of a solution is higher than that of the pure solvent.
K_b is the molal boiling point elevation constant.

flashcards.title: Depression in Freezing Point
explanation: The freezing point of a solution is lower than that of the pure solvent.
K_f is the molal freezing point depression constant.

flashcards.title: Osmotic Pressure
explanation: Osmotic pressure is the pressure required to stop the flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane.

flashcards.title: Abnormal Colligative Properties (Van't Hoff Correction Factor)
explanation: Van't Hoff factor accounts for the effect of ionization or association on colligative properties.

flashcards.title: Relative Lowering of Vapor Pressure
formulas: RLVP = ΔP / P = X_solute = n / (n + N)
RLVP = (i × molality × M) / 1000 (M = molar mass of solvent)
explanation: Relative lowering of vapor pressure is a colligative property dependent on the number of solute particles in a solution.

flashcards.title: Henry's Law
formulas: m ∝ P (m = mass of gas dissolved, P = pressure of gas)
explanation: Henry's law relates the solubility of a gas in a liquid to the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid.

flashcards.title: Ideal and Non-Ideal Solutions
explanation: Ideal solutions follow Raoult's law at all compositions, while non-ideal solutions show deviations due to interactions between components.

flashcards.title: Immiscible Liquids
formulas: P_A° / P_B° = W_B M_A / W_A M_B
explanation: The total vapor pressure of immiscible liquids is the sum of the vapor pressures of the components.

flashcards.title: Classification of Crystal into Seven Systems
formulas: Cubic: a = b = c; α = β = γ = 90°
Orthorhombic: a ≠ b ≠ c; α = β = γ = 90°
Tetragonal: a = b ≠ c; α = β = γ = 90°
Monoclinic: a ≠ b ≠ c; α = γ = 90°, β ≠ 90°
Rhombohedral: a = b = c; α = β = γ ≠ 90°
Triclinic: a ≠ b ≠ c; α ≠ β ≠ γ
Hexagonal: a = b ≠ c; α = β = 90°, γ = 120°
explanation: Crystals are classified based on unit cell dimensions and angles into seven systems.

flashcards.title: Analysis of Cubical System
formulas: SC (Simple Cubic): r = a/2, Packing Efficiency = 52%
FCC (Face-Centered Cubic): r = a/√2, Packing Efficiency = 74%
explanation: Cubic systems are analyzed for atomic radius (r), packing efficiency, and number of atoms per unit cell.

flashcards.title: Density of Lattice Matter
explanation: Density of a crystal lattice depends on the number of atoms per unit cell (Z), molar mass (M), and edge length (a).

flashcards.title: Ionic Crystals
explanation: Ionic crystals are categorized based on limiting radius ratio and coordination number.

flashcards.title: Crystal Defects (Imperfections)
formulas: Stoichiometric Defects: Schottky (ion pairs missing), Frenkel (dislocation of ions)
Non-Stoichiometric Defects: Metal Excess (extra cation or electron), Non-Metal Excess (extra anion or electron)
explanation: Crystal defects include point defects such as vacancies (Schottky) and dislocations (Frenkel), as well as non-stoichiometric defects involving excess ions or electrons.

flashcards.title: Examples of Ionic Crystals
explanation: Examples of ionic crystals are categorized by their coordination numbers and structural characteristics.

flashcards.title: Rate/Velocity of Chemical Reaction
formulas: Average rate = Total change in concentration / Total time taken
explanation: Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of reactants or products over time.

flashcards.title: Rate Law
explanation: Rate law expresses the relationship between the reaction rate and the concentrations of reactants.

flashcards.title: Integrated Rate Laws
explanation: Integrated rate laws provide equations to calculate concentrations at a given time.

flashcards.title: Methods to Determine Order of Reaction
explanation: Order of reaction can be determined using experimental data.

flashcards.title: Effect of Temperature on Rate of Reaction
explanation: Rate of reaction increases with temperature due to greater molecular collisions.

flashcards.title: Methods to Monitor Progress of Reaction
formulas: Gaseous reaction: k = (2.303 / t) * log(P_0 / P)
Titration method: k = (2.303 / t) * log(V_0 / V_t)
explanation: Various methods are used to track reaction progress depending on the reaction type.

flashcards.title: Arrhenius Theory
formulas: ln k = ln A - Ea / RT
explanation: Arrhenius theory relates the rate constant to activation energy and temperature.

flashcards.title: Shielding or Screening Effect
explanation: The larger the number of electrons in the inner shells, the greater the shielding effect, reducing nuclear attraction and lowering ionization energy.

flashcards.title: Penetration Effect
explanation: For the same energy level, the order of penetration effect is: s > p > d > f. Higher penetration results in higher ionization energy.

flashcards.title: Electron Gain Enthalpy
explanation: Electron gain enthalpy measures the energy change when an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom.
Halogens have high negative electron gain enthalpies, whereas noble gases have large positive values.

flashcards.title: Electronegativity
explanation: Electronegativity measures the tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons in a covalent bond.
Pauling’s scale and Mulliken’s scale are commonly used to quantify electronegativity.

flashcards.title: Periodicity of Valence or Oxidation States
explanation: Variable valence is characteristic of transition elements and actinides.
Across a period, oxidation states increase, while they decrease within a group.

flashcards.title: Periodic Trends in Oxides
explanation: In a group, oxides become more basic down the group.
In a period, oxides change from basic to acidic moving from left to right.

flashcards.title: Effective Nuclear Charge
explanation: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge experienced by valence electrons, considering shielding effects.

flashcards.title: Atomic Radius
explanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period due to increasing nuclear charge, and increases down a group due to added electron shells.

flashcards.title: Ionic Radius
explanation: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms due to loss of electrons, while anions are larger due to electron gain.

flashcards.title: Ionization Energy
explanation: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
It increases across a period and decreases down a group.

flashcards.title: s-Block Elements
explanation: Includes Group 1 and 2 elements with a general configuration of [noble gas]ns¹-².
These elements are highly reactive and form basic oxides.

flashcards.title: p-Block Elements
explanation: Groups 13 to 18 elements, with general configuration [noble gas]ns²np¹-⁶.
They show variable oxidation states and include metals, non-metals, and metalloids.

flashcards.title: d-Block Elements
explanation: Transition metals with partially filled d-orbitals exhibit variable oxidation states, forming colored compounds and acting as catalysts.

flashcards.title: f-Block Elements
explanation: Lanthanides and actinides are characterized by the filling of f-orbitals and show similar chemical properties.

flashcards.title: Dipole Moment
explanation: Dipole moment represents the shift in electron density, shown by crossed arrows above the Lewis structure.
Non-zero summation of moment vectors in a molecule results in a dipole moment.

flashcards.title: Resonance
explanation: Resonance involves multiple structures with identical atom positions for a compound.
The ozone (O₃) molecule can be equally represented by multiple resonance structures.

flashcards.title: Resonance Hybrid
explanation: Represents the actual structure combining all possible resonance forms.
Example: Benzene's resonance hybrid structure.

flashcards.title: Conditions for H-Bond
explanation: Requires electronegative atoms (F, O, N) linked to H-atoms.
Smaller size of electronegative atom ensures stronger bonding.
Presence of lone pairs on electronegative atoms is necessary.

flashcards.title: Types of Hydrogen Bonds
explanation: Intramolecular H-Bonding: Occurs within the same molecule, e.g., o-hydroxybenzaldehyde.
Intermolecular H-Bonding: Formed between molecules, e.g., in water (H₂O) and HF.

flashcards.title: Sigma and Pi Bonds
explanation: Sigma bonds involve head-on overlapping of orbitals, e.g., s-s, s-p, or p-p overlaps.
Pi bonds involve lateral overlap of p-orbitals.

flashcards.title: VSEPR Theory
explanation: Explains molecular shape based on electron pair repulsion around the central atom.

flashcards.title: Hybridization
explanation: Hybrid orbitals form by combining atomic orbitals of similar energy.
Types: sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d².

flashcards.title: Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT)
explanation: Molecular orbitals are formed by the combination of atomic orbitals, influencing bonding and antibonding characteristics.

flashcards.title: Definition
explanation: Coordination compounds are formed by the combination of two or more stable compounds in stoichiometric ratios.

flashcards.title: Double Salts
explanation: Compounds that lose their identity in solution, e.g., K2SO4, Al2(SO4)3.

flashcards.title: Central Atom/Ion
explanation: The atom or ion to which ligands are bound in a coordination entity.

flashcards.title: Ligands
explanation: Neutral molecules, anions, or cations directly linked to the central atom in a definite geometrical arrangement.

flashcards.title: Chelate Ligand
explanation: A ligand that uses two or more donor atoms to bind a metal ion.

flashcards.title: Ambidentate Ligands
explanation: Ligands that can link through two different atoms, such as nitrito-N (NO2-) or nitrito-O.

flashcards.title: Coordination Number
explanation: The number of donor atoms directly attached to the metal.

flashcards.title: Oxidation Number of Central Atom
explanation: The charge the central atom would carry if all ligands were removed.

flashcards.title: Werner’s Theory
explanation: Primary and secondary valences define the oxidation state and coordination number.
Primary valence corresponds to the oxidation state, and secondary valence corresponds to the coordination number.

flashcards.title: Common Ligands Table
explanation: Table of common ligands such as methyl isocyanide, ethylenediamine, and more, categorized by denticity.

flashcards.title: Nomenclature Rules
explanation: Central atom is placed first, followed by ligands in alphabetical order.
The oxidation state of the central atom is denoted by Roman numerals in parentheses.

flashcards.title: Valence Bond Theory (VBT)
explanation: Utilizes hybridization of metal orbitals for bonding and geometry prediction.
Hybridization types include sp3, sp3d2, dsp3, and others.

flashcards.title: Magnetic Moment
explanation: μ is determined by the number of unpaired electrons in the d-orbitals.

flashcards.title: Crystal Field Theory (CFT)
explanation: CFT explains the splitting of d-orbitals in a crystal field into lower and higher energy levels.
Splitting depends on the geometry and nature of ligands.

flashcards.title: Calculation of CFSE
explanation: CFSE calculates the stabilization energy due to crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes.

flashcards.title: Stability of Coordination Compounds
explanation: Stability constants (βn) are used to measure the stability of coordination compounds.
Higher βn indicates greater stability.

flashcards.title: Isomerism in Coordination Compounds
explanation: Structural Isomerism includes ionization, solvate, linkage, and coordination isomerism.
Stereoisomerism includes geometrical and optical isomerism.

flashcards.title: Definition
explanation: Compounds containing metal-carbon bonds are called organometallic compounds.

flashcards.title: Types of Bonds
explanation: Sigma-bonded organometallic compounds include Grignard's reagent.
Pi-bonded organometallic compounds include Zeise's salt, ferrocene.

flashcards.title: Synergic Bonding
explanation: Involves donation of electron density from the ligand to the metal and back donation from the metal to the ligand.

flashcards.title: Examples
explanation: Examples include Grignard's reagent (R-Mg-X), Zeise's salt, ferrocene, and others.

flashcards.title: Definition of Minerals and Ores
explanation: Minerals are naturally occurring compounds of metals found in nature.
Ores are minerals from which metals can be economically and conveniently extracted.

flashcards.title: Types of Ores
explanation: Native ores: Metals in free state (e.g., silver, gold, platinum).
Oxidized ores: Contain oxides or oxy-salts (e.g., carbonates, phosphates).
Sulphide ores: Contain sulphides (e.g., iron pyrite, copper pyrite).
Halide ores: Contain halides (e.g., chlorargyrite).

flashcards.title: Crushing and Grinding
explanation: The ore is crushed and ground to a fine powder for further processing.

flashcards.title: Concentration of Ore
explanation: Hydraulic washing: Based on differences in density between ore and gangue particles.
Electromagnetic separation: Uses magnetic properties of ore components.
Froth flotation: Used for sulphide ores, where gangue particles are wetted by water and ore particles by oil.
Leaching: Dissolves ore in a suitable solvent for further extraction.

flashcards.title: Conversion of Ore to Oxide
explanation: Calcination: Heating the ore in limited air to remove water and volatile impurities.
Roasting: Heating the ore in excess air to convert sulphide ores to oxides.

flashcards.title: Reduction of Oxides to Metals
explanation: Chemical reduction: Using reducing agents like carbon or CO.
Electrolytic reduction: Used for highly reactive metals like aluminum.

flashcards.title: Extraction of Aluminum
explanation: Involves Bayer’s process for purification of bauxite and Hall-Heroult process for electrolytic reduction of alumina.

flashcards.title: Refining of Metals
explanation: Liquation: Removes impurities from metals with low melting points (e.g., tin, zinc).
Electrolytic refining: Produces pure metals like copper and aluminum.
Vapor phase refining: Includes Mond’s process for nickel and Van Arkel process for titanium.

flashcards.title: Key Extraction Reactions
explanation: Extraction of zinc, tin, and slag formation reactions during smelting processes.

flashcards.title: Purification Methods
explanation: Zone refining: Used for semiconductors like Si and Ge.
Poling: Used for removing impurities from metals like copper.

flashcards.title: Physical Properties of Alkali Metals
explanation: Alkali metals are silvery white, soft, and light.
They exhibit low density and melting points.
Their salts impart characteristic colors to a flame: Li - crimson red, Na - yellow, K - violet, Rb - red violet, Cs - blue.

flashcards.title: Chemical Properties of Alkali Metals
explanation: Alkali metals are highly reactive due to their large atomic size and low ionization enthalpy.
They react with water to form hydroxides and hydrogen gas.
React with oxygen to form oxides, peroxides, or superoxides.

flashcards.title: Properties of Alkaline Earth Metals
explanation: Alkaline earth metals have higher melting and boiling points than alkali metals.
They are harder and denser than alkali metals.
Their salts impart characteristic colors to a flame: Ca - brick red, Sr - crimson, Ba - apple green.

flashcards.title: Reactivity of Alkaline Earth Metals
explanation: React with water to form hydroxides and hydrogen gas.
Form ionic oxides and chlorides.
Beryllium and magnesium react less vigorously due to their smaller atomic size.

flashcards.title: Diagonal Relationship of Lithium and Magnesium
explanation: Lithium resembles magnesium in properties due to a similar charge/radius ratio.
Both form nitrides (Li₃N, Mg₃N₂), carbonates, and hydroxides that decompose on heating.

flashcards.title: Uses of s-block Elements
explanation: Sodium is used in streetlights, nuclear reactors, and as a heat exchanger.
Potassium is used in fertilizers and fireworks.
Calcium is used in construction (lime and cement) and in reducing agents.

flashcards.title: Compounds of Sodium
explanation: Sodium carbonate is used in glass manufacturing.
Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is used in soap making and water purification.

flashcards.title: Compounds of Calcium
explanation: Quick lime (CaO) is used in cement production.
Slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂) is used in water softening and as a whitewash.
Bleaching powder (Ca(OCl)₂) is used for disinfection.

flashcards.title: Trends in Properties of p-Block Elements
formulas: Oxidation states vary across the groups
explanation: p-Block elements exhibit diverse properties due to varying oxidation states.
Electronegativity generally decreases down the group, while metallic character increases.

flashcards.title: Boron Family (Group 13)
explanation: The general oxidation state is +3.
Reactivity includes reaction with acids and alkalis to form corresponding salts and hydrogen gas.

flashcards.title: Important Reactions of Boron
explanation: Boron forms compounds like boron trifluoride and reacts with magnesium to produce elemental boron.

flashcards.title: Carbon Family (Group 14)
explanation: Carbon and silicon are key members of Group 14.
Oxidation states range from -4 to +4, and these elements form oxides and halides.

flashcards.title: Allotropes of Carbon
explanation: Carbon exhibits allotropy, forming structures like diamond (tetrahedral network) and graphite (layered hexagonal).

flashcards.title: Nitrogen Family (Group 15)
explanation: Group 15 elements show oxidation states of -3, +3, and +5.
Nitrogen forms ammonia, while phosphorus forms oxides and other compounds.

flashcards.title: Oxygen Family (Group 16)
explanation: Oxygen and sulfur are prominent elements in Group 16.
They exhibit oxidation states of -2, +4, and +6, forming oxides and sulfides.

flashcards.title: Halogen Family (Group 17)
explanation: Halogens exhibit -1 oxidation state and react with metals to form salts.
They also form interhalogen and oxo-compounds.

flashcards.title: Noble Gases (Group 18)
explanation: Noble gases are chemically inert but can form compounds under extreme conditions.
Xenon forms fluorides and oxides in controlled reactions.

flashcards.title: Potassium Permanganate (KMnO₄)
explanation: KMnO₄ is an oxidizing agent in both acidic and alkaline mediums.
In acidic medium, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺, while in alkaline medium, it forms MnO₂.

flashcards.title: Potassium Dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇)
explanation: Potassium dichromate is used as an oxidizing agent in acidic medium.
It can oxidize Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and I⁻ to I₂.

flashcards.title: Formation of Colored Ions
explanation: Transition metal ions appear colored due to d-d electronic transitions.
The observed color is complementary to the absorbed wavelength.

flashcards.title: Magnetic Properties
explanation: Substances with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic, while those without are diamagnetic.

flashcards.title: Catalytic Properties
explanation: Transition metals and their compounds act as catalysts due to variable oxidation states and large surface areas.

flashcards.title: Alloy Formation
explanation: Transition metals form alloys due to their similar atomic sizes.

flashcards.title: Oxidation States
explanation: Transition elements show variable oxidation states due to the involvement of (n-1)d and ns electrons in bonding.

flashcards.title: IVth Group (Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺, Ni²⁺, Co²⁺)
explanation: In the IVth group, sulfides are precipitated using H₂S in an alkaline medium.
ZnS, MnS, NiS, and CoS precipitates are formed and further analyzed.
ZnS and MnS are confirmed using specific reagents like ammonium carbonate and dilute acids, while CoS and NiS are tested using aqua regia and dimethylglyoxime.

flashcards.title: Vth Group (Ba²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ca²⁺)
explanation: The Vth group involves precipitating carbonates using ammonium carbonate in the presence of ammonia.
Tests for confirmation include reactions with K₂CrO₄ (yellow BaCrO₄ precipitate), (NH₄)₂SO₄ (white SrSO₄ precipitate), and (NH₄)₂C₂O₄ (white CaC₂O₄ precipitate).

flashcards.title: VIth Group (Mg²⁺)
formulas: Mg(OH)₂ + Titan Yellow → Deep red precipitate
explanation: Magnesium ions are confirmed using ammonium phosphate, forming Mg(NH₄)PO₄.
Titan yellow dye is used to produce a deep red precipitate with Mg(OH)₂, further confirming the presence of Mg²⁺ ions.

flashcards.title: Chloride Ion (Cl⁻)
formulas: Cl⁻ + Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H⁺ → CrO₂Cl₂ (deep red vapors)
explanation: Concentrated H₂SO₄ reacts with chlorides to produce HCl gas, which is pungent.
Silver nitrate test produces a white precipitate of AgCl, soluble in ammonia.
Chromyl chloride test produces deep red vapors of CrO₂Cl₂.

flashcards.title: Bromide Ion (Br⁻)
explanation: Bromide ions react with concentrated H₂SO₄ to produce reddish-brown vapors of bromine.
Silver nitrate test forms a pale yellow precipitate of AgBr.
Chlorine water can oxidize bromide to bromine, which can dissolve in an organic layer.

flashcards.title: Iodide Ion (I⁻)
explanation: Iodide ions react with concentrated H₂SO₄ to produce violet fumes of iodine.
Silver nitrate test forms a bright yellow precipitate of AgI, insoluble in ammonia.
Chlorine water test produces violet color in the organic layer due to iodine dissolution.

flashcards.title: Charcoal Cavity Test
explanation: Residues formed during heating in the charcoal cavity test help identify specific cations.
Yellow (Zn²⁺), brown (Cu²⁺), and white (general salts) residues are common observations.

flashcards.title: Cobalt Nitrate Test
explanation: When specific metals are treated with cobalt nitrate, distinct colored masses form.
Zinc forms green, aluminum forms blue, and magnesium forms pink masses.

flashcards.title: Flame Test
explanation: Characteristic flame colors include crimson red (Li⁺), golden yellow (Na⁺), violet (K⁺), and green (Ba²⁺).
The flame color is due to electronic transitions within metal cations.

flashcards.title: Borax Bead Test
explanation: When metals are treated in an oxidizing or reducing flame with borax, different colors appear.
Copper produces green (oxidizing) and colorless (reducing) colors, while cobalt produces blue in both flames.

flashcards.title: IUPAC System of Nomenclature
formulas: Secondary Prefix + Primary Prefix + Word Root + Primary Suffix + Secondary Suffix
explanation: IUPAC names consist of several parts to define the molecular structure and functional groups.
For example: CH3-CH2-OH → Ethanol.

flashcards.title: Common and IUPAC Names
explanation: CH3-CH=CH2 → Propylene (Common) / Propene (IUPAC)
CH3-C≡CH → Methyl acetylene (Common) / Propyne (IUPAC)

flashcards.title: Functional Group Names
explanation: Functional groups determine the suffix in IUPAC nomenclature.
Example: CH3COOH → Ethanoic acid.

flashcards.title: Isopropyl Alcohol
explanation: Isopropyl alcohol is used as a solvent and antiseptic.

flashcards.title: Toluene
explanation: Toluene is used in industrial applications as a solvent and chemical intermediate.

flashcards.title: Glycerol
explanation: Glycerol is a viscous liquid used in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics.

flashcards.title: Chain Isomers
explanation: Chain isomers have different sizes of main chains or side chains.
Condition: They have the same nature of locants.

flashcards.title: Positional Isomers
explanation: Positional isomers have different positions of locants.
Condition: They should have the same size of the main chain and same side chain and nature of locants.

flashcards.title: Functional Isomers
explanation: Functional isomers have different nature of locants.
Condition: Chain and positional isomerism is not considered.

flashcards.title: Metamerism
explanation: Metamers have different nature of alkyl groups along a polyvalent functional group.
Condition: They should have the same nature of functional groups, chain & positional isomerism is ignored.

flashcards.title: Tautomerism
explanation: Tautomers have different positions of hydrogen atoms.
Condition: The two functional isomers remain in dynamic equilibrium to each other.

flashcards.title: Conjugation between C=C and C=C
explanation: Occurs due to interaction of π-electrons of two double bonds.

flashcards.title: Conjugation between C=C and Positive Charge
explanation: Interaction of π-electrons with an adjacent positively charged atom.

flashcards.title: Conjugation between Lone Pair and C=C
explanation: Occurs when lone pair electrons on an atom interact with a double bond.

flashcards.title: Conjugation between Odd Electron and C=C
explanation: Interaction between π-electrons and an unpaired electron.

flashcards.title: Conjugation between Negative Charge and C=C
explanation: Occurs due to delocalization of π-electrons with a negative charge.

flashcards.title: Hyperconjugation in Alkenes
explanation: Delocalization of sigma electrons with p-orbitals in alkenes.

flashcards.title: Hyperconjugation in Carbocations
explanation: Involves overlap of sigma bonds with an adjacent empty p-orbital.

flashcards.title: Hyperconjugation in Free Radicals
explanation: Delocalization of sigma electrons with a radical site.

flashcards.title: Inductive Effect
explanation: The inductive effect is a permanent displacement of σ-bond electrons due to differences in electronegativity.
It operates through σ bonds and diminishes with distance from the source of the effect.
Types: -I Effect (electron-withdrawing groups like NO₂, CN) and +I Effect (electron-donating groups like alkyl groups).

flashcards.title: Resonance
formulas: Resonance hybrid of CH₂=CH-CH=CH₂: All structures contribute to a hybrid with delocalized π electrons.
explanation: Resonance involves delocalization of π electrons across adjacent multiple bonds or lone pairs, increasing stability.
The resonance hybrid represents the molecule's most stable form.

flashcards.title: Conjugation
explanation: Conjugation occurs in systems with alternating single and double bonds, lone pairs, or empty p orbitals.
Examples include CH₂=CH-CH=CH₂ and benzene.

flashcards.title: Hyperconjugation
explanation: Hyperconjugation involves delocalization of σ electrons of C-H bonds adjacent to a double bond or carbocation.
It is also known as no-bond resonance.

flashcards.title: Free Radicals
explanation: Free radicals are neutral species with unpaired electrons, formed by homolytic bond cleavage.
They are stabilized by resonance, hyperconjugation, and inductive effects.

flashcards.title: Carbenes
explanation: Carbenes are divalent carbon intermediates with a lone pair and an incomplete octet.
They are highly reactive and can be stabilized through resonance.

flashcards.title: Nitrenes
explanation: Nitrenes are nitrogen analogs of carbenes with one unpaired electron.
They are highly reactive due to incomplete octets.

flashcards.title: Aromatic Character
explanation: Aromatic compounds are cyclic, planar, and contain (4n + 2)π electrons in a delocalized π system.
Examples include benzene and naphthalene.

flashcards.title: Carbocations
explanation: Carbocations are positively charged carbon species stabilized by resonance, inductive effects, and hyperconjugation.
Stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl.

flashcards.title: Carbanions
explanation: Carbanions are negatively charged carbon species stabilized by resonance and inductive effects.
Stability order: methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary.

flashcards.title: Benzyne
explanation: Benzyne is a highly reactive intermediate with a strained triple bond within the benzene ring.
It is generated in elimination-addition reactions.

flashcards.title: Mechanism of Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution
explanation: An electron withdrawing group at ortho or para positions with respect to a good leaving group is necessary for S_N2Ar reactions.
Intermediate ions are stabilized by resonance and form stable salts called Meisenheimer salts.
Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the carbanion by dispersing negative charge, activating the reaction.
Electron-releasing groups destabilize the carbanion, slowing down the reaction.

flashcards.title: Element Effect in S_N2Ar
formulas: Reactivity order: Ar-F > Ar-Cl > Ar-Br > Ar-I
explanation: Reactivity depends on the halogen attached to the aromatic ring due to its electron-withdrawing nature.

chapters.name: Reactions of Alkanes, Alkenes, and Alkynes

flashcards.title: Wurtz Reaction
explanation: The reaction of primary or secondary alkyl halides with sodium in ether to form alkanes.

flashcards.title: Electrophilic Addition in Alkenes and Alkynes
explanation: Alkenes and alkynes undergo electrophilic addition reactions, forming carbocation intermediates.
The major product follows Markovnikov's rule when unsymmetrical reagents are added.

flashcards.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions
explanation: S_N1: Two-step mechanism involving carbocation intermediate.
S_N2: One-step mechanism involving a backside attack and inversion of configuration.

flashcards.title: Williamson's Ether Synthesis
explanation: Involves the reaction of alcohol with alkyl halide in the presence of a base to form ethers.

flashcards.title: Grignard Reagent and Its Reactions
formulas: Cyclic ester + 2 RMgX → Ring alcohol (2° or 3° depending on structure)
explanation: Grignard reagents (RMgX) are organomagnesium halides used in organic synthesis.
They react with aldehydes to form primary alcohols, ketones to form secondary alcohols, and esters to form tertiary alcohols.
Grignard reagents also react with CO₂ to produce carboxylic acids.
Cyclic esters undergo ring opening with Grignard reagents, producing alcohols.

flashcards.title: LiAlH₄ Reduction
explanation: LiAlH₄ is a strong reducing agent that reduces aldehydes, carboxylic acids, ketones, and nitriles to their respective alcohols or amines.
It is commonly used in organic synthesis for selective reductions.

flashcards.title: NaBH₄ Reduction
explanation: NaBH₄ selectively reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols.
It is a milder reducing agent compared to LiAlH₄.

flashcards.title: Bouvet Blanc Reduction
explanation: Bouvet Blanc reduction utilizes sodium in alcohol as the reducing agent, capable of reducing various carbonyl compounds and esters.

flashcards.title: Clemmensen Reduction
explanation: Clemmensen reduction uses Zn-Hg in HCl to reduce carbonyl groups (ketones and aldehydes) to methylene groups.
It is suitable for compounds stable in acidic conditions.

flashcards.title: Wolff-Kishner Reduction
explanation: Wolff-Kishner reduction involves hydrazine (NH₂-NH₂) and KOH to reduce carbonyl groups to methylene groups.
It is used for compounds stable under basic conditions.

flashcards.title: Birch Reduction
explanation: Birch reduction uses alkali metals in liquid ammonia to reduce alkynes to trans alkenes.
Terminal alkynes are not reduced.

flashcards.title: Oxidation Reaction
explanation: Various reagents like KMnO₄, PCC, Cu, etc., are used for oxidizing alcohols, aldehydes, and alkenes into acids, ketones, or other oxidized products.
Periodic acid cleaves vicinal diols into aldehydes or ketones.
Baeyer’s reagent results in stereospecific syn addition to form diols.
Prilezhaev reaction involves anti hydroxylation to form diols.
MnO₂ specifically oxidizes allylic and benzylic alcohols.

flashcards.title: Reduction Reaction
explanation: LiAlH₄ and NaBH₄ reduce aldehydes, ketones, esters, and acid chlorides to alcohols.
Rosenmund’s reduction selectively reduces acid chlorides to aldehydes.
Birch reduction converts alkynes to trans-alkenes using metal in liquid ammonia.
Stephen’s reduction reduces nitriles to aldehydes.
Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner reductions convert ketones to alkanes under acidic or basic conditions respectively.
DIBAL-H selectively reduces esters to aldehydes at low temperature.

flashcards.title: Aldol Condensation
explanation: Carbonyl compounds having acidic sp² α-H show aldol condensation in the presence of dilute NaOH or dilute acid.

flashcards.title: Cannizzaro Reaction
explanation: Carbonyl compounds without sp² α-H undergo Cannizzaro reaction, involving disproportionation in the presence of NaOH.

flashcards.title: Perkin Reaction
explanation: An aromatic aldehyde reacts with the anhydride of an aliphatic acid in the presence of its sodium salt to form an α, β-unsaturated acid.

flashcards.title: Haloform Reaction
explanation: Acetaldehyde and methyl ketones react with halogens in the presence of alkali to produce haloform.

flashcards.title: LiAlH₄ Reduction
explanation: LiAlH₄ reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and carboxylic acids to primary alcohols.

flashcards.title: NaBH₄ Reduction
explanation: NaBH₄ selectively reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols.

flashcards.title: Birch Reduction
explanation: Alkynes are reduced to trans alkenes using Na/NH₃.

flashcards.title: KMnO₄ Oxidation
explanation: KMnO₄ oxidizes primary alcohols and aldehydes to carboxylic acids.

flashcards.title: PCC Oxidation
explanation: PCC selectively oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes.

flashcards.title: Prilezhaev Reaction
explanation: Alkenes react with MCPBA to form epoxides, followed by hydrolysis to diols.

flashcards.title: Hydrolysis of Esters
explanation: In acidic medium or with water, esters hydrolyze to give carboxylic acid and alcohol.

flashcards.title: Saponification
explanation: When treated with NaOH, esters undergo saponification, yielding soap and alcohol.

flashcards.title: Aminolysis
explanation: Reaction of esters with ammonia results in the formation of amides and alcohol.

flashcards.title: Bouvaeu-Blanc Reduction
explanation: In the presence of Na/alcohol, esters are reduced to primary alcohols.

flashcards.title: Reaction with Na Metal
explanation: Carboxylic acids react with sodium metal to produce sodium carboxylate and hydrogen gas.

flashcards.title: Reaction with SOCl₂
explanation: Carboxylic acids react with thionyl chloride to produce acid chlorides.

flashcards.title: Hydrolysis of Acid Chlorides
explanation: Acid chlorides react with water to yield carboxylic acids and hydrochloric acid.

flashcards.title: Reaction with Alcohols
explanation: Acid chlorides react with alcohols to form esters.

flashcards.title: Hofmann Bromide Reaction
explanation: Amides react with bromine in the presence of KOH to yield amines.

flashcards.title: Reduction with LiAlH₄
explanation: Amides can be reduced to primary amines using lithium aluminium hydride.

flashcards.title: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
formulas: Formation of electrophile: Br2 + FeBr3 → Br⁺ + FeBr4⁻
explanation: The process involves generating an electrophile that reacts with benzene to form a sigma complex, followed by proton loss to restore aromaticity.
Examples include Bromination, Nitration, and Sulphonation.

flashcards.title: Friedel-Craft Reactions
explanation: Alkylation introduces alkyl groups into benzene, while acylation introduces acyl groups using acid chlorides and Lewis acids.
Note: Acylations prevent multiple substitutions.

flashcards.title: Chemical Reactions of Benzene
formulas: Halogenation: C6H6 + Cl2 → C6H5Cl + HCl (in presence of FeCl3)
explanation: Benzene undergoes reactions like nitration, sulphonation, and halogenation under specific conditions.

flashcards.title: Hydrolysis
explanation: Ester hydrolysis in acidic medium produces carboxylic acid and alcohol.

flashcards.title: Saponification
explanation: Saponification involves ester hydrolysis in the presence of a base, forming soap (carboxylate salt) and alcohol.

flashcards.title: Reduction of Esters
formulas: R-COOR' + 2[H] → R-CH2OH + R'-OH (using LiAlH4 or Na/Alcohol)
explanation: Esters are reduced to primary alcohols using reducing agents like LiAlH4 or sodium in alcohol.

flashcards.title: Polyethylene (LDPE and HDPE)
explanation: LDPE: Produced by free radical polymerization, used in film wraps and plastic bags.
HDPE: Produced by Ziegler-Natta polymerization, used in toys and electrical insulation.

flashcards.title: Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC)
explanation: Produced from vinyl chloride monomers, used in raincoats and water pipes.

flashcards.title: Polystyrene
explanation: Produced from styrene, used as insulating and packing material.

flashcards.title: Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, Teflon)
explanation: Produced from tetrafluoroethylene, used in non-stick surfaces and electrical insulation.

flashcards.title: Polyester (Dacron or Terylene)
explanation: Produced from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, used in fabrics and tire cords.

flashcards.title: Nylon-6,6
explanation: Produced from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, used in parachutes and clothing.

flashcards.title: Bakelite
explanation: Produced from phenol and formaldehyde, used in electrical switches and combs.

flashcards.title: Poly-β-hydroxybutyrate-co-β-hydroxyvalerate (PHBV)
explanation: Used in packaging and controlled drug release, degrades in the environment via bacterial action.

flashcards.title: Nylon-2-Nylon-6
explanation: Alternating polyamide copolymer of glycine and amino caproic acid, used as biodegradable polymer.
